title: Building Great Teams Raising the Bar
author: Dominic Salles
summary: In Chapter 10 of his Head of Department Manifesto, Dominic Salles uses Bartlett's three-bar test: imagine a team made entirely of one teacher and ask whether it would raise, hold or lower the bar. He shows why tolerating a talented maverick is costly, since a 10 percent drop in team effectiveness across a cohort of 200 means roughly 20 more pupils missing a grade that one teacher cannot realistically recover. A story about a gifted unqualified Shakespeare teacher who was pushed out illustrates how a school can lose a maverick it never chose to fire. His central claim is that leaders fix people first when they should work in order through structure, then team culture, then interpersonal dynamics, and only last the individual. Skills and self-awareness are coachable, he says, leaving character as the true residue, to be handled with the same coaching questions used for student behaviour.
points: The three-bar test asks whether a team made entirely of one person's values would raise, hold or lower the bar, which exposes the hidden cost of mavericks.
A maverick who cuts team effectiveness by 10 percent would need about 20 pupils a full grade above prediction just to break even, a deficit few can cover.
Most team problems are structural, so leaders should fix goals, expectations and culture before judging individuals.
Interpersonal tension is best handled by anchoring conflict to impact on learning, and character issues by the coaching checklist used with students.
quotes: Name a person in your team. What values do they have? Now imagine everyone else in the team had those same values. What would that do to your team?

But, if the team becomes even 10% less effective, in a cohort of 200, 20 more students will miss a grade. To counter that effect, the maverick would need their class to contain 20 students who each scored a full grade above predicted. If the team is just 15% less effective, that figure now becomes 30 students in the maverick’s class who would need to get an extra grade, just for the team to stand still.
Beau wasn’t fired, or forced out on purpose. He was forced out by becoming a maverick.
Unlike a business, we can’t simply fire a maverick. But we can do two things – bring them into the fold, or make them realise they need a different team.
This is completely the wrong focus – we must end up at the individual last.
The solution to any character problem is the same as the solution to students who cannot change their behaviour.
